lesson.title: Capstone: Le Pont Reading
lesson.subtitle: Walking across Le Pont in Paris — every conversion bridge, tense frame, and left-walking pronoun in one living story

hook.title: Look How Much French Was Already Inside Your Head
hook.content: Read this Paris paragraph out loud and watch every topic from the trail light up at once: 'J'habite à Paris depuis deux ans. Hier, quand je suis sorti de l'hôtel, j'ai vu mon ami qui est professeur à l'université. Il m'a dit : « Il faut célébrer ce soir ! J'ai réservé une table au restaurant dont tu parles. » Naturellement, j'ai répondu : « Tu as raison, j'ai très faim — on y va ! »' Every single clause is built from the 9 conversion bridges and the mental-theatre rules you now own.

footnotes.title: Why you never needed a phrasebook
footnotes.content: A phrasebook hands you frozen sentences you cannot alter. A conversion engine hands you the blueprint so you can build sentences you have never heard before.

pattern.title: The Nine Bridges and Five Engines in One Glance
pattern.content: You now hold the complete architecture of Le Pont: (1) The 9 Vocabulary Bridges (-ion, -ation→-er, -ité, -ance, -é↔-ed, -ment, -eur, -able, and Norman doublets like hôtel/hospital). (2) The Left-Walking Pronouns (le, la, lui, leur, me, te, se, y, en). (3) The Ne...Pas Sandwich. (4) The Four Time Frames (Present + depuis, Near Future je vais + inf, Passé Composé avoir/être + participle, Imparfait -ais/-ait). (5) The Polite & Necessary Moods (je voudrais, il faut que).
pattern.linguist_note: English is the most Latinized Germanic language in the world; French is the most Germanicized Romance language — which makes the Channel the richest cognate bridge on earth.
pattern.trap_note: Never revert to translating English word-for-word when under pressure: pause, picture the thought (who acts? does a pronoun walk left? is the state possessed with avoir?), and let the French engine assemble it.

exercises.prompt: Match each conversion bridge from the course with its flagship example:

matching_pairs.german: j'y vais / j'en veux / je lui parle

exercises.target_answer: la réservation / l'université, confirmation → confirmer, exactement / naturellement, j'ai vu / c'était, j'y vais / j'en veux / je lui parle
exercises.meaning: -ION & -ITÉ (100% feminine), -ATION → -ER verb engine, -LY → -MENT adverb bridge, Passé composé + Imparfait, Left-walking pronouns (y / en / lui)
exercises.explanation: All nine bridges and five syntactic engines work together in real French.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'Il m'a dit qu'il faut partir'?
exercises.german: Il m'a dit qu'il faut partir
exercises.natural: He told me that we have to leave
options: He me told that one must leaving
He to-me has said that it is-needed to-leave
He told me that we have to leave
exercises.target_answer: He to-me has said that it is-needed to-leave
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: He to-me has said that it is-needed to-leave
exercises.explanation: m' ('to me') walks before a dit ('has said'), and qu'il faut partir expresses necessity.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentences capture the full meaning of 'J'habite ici depuis trois ans et j'adore la ville'?
exercises.german: J'habite ici depuis trois ans et j'adore la ville
exercises.meaning: I have been living here for three years and I love the city
renderings: I've lived here for three years and I love the city
I have been living here for three years and I adore the town
traps: I lived here three years ago and left the city
I am going to live here for three years
exercises.target_answer: I've lived here for three years and I love the city
exercises.explanation: Present tense + depuis shows the three-year stay is still ongoing today.

exercises.idea: I would like to reserve a table because we are going to celebrate tonight
cues: Je voudrais réserver une table parce que nous allons célébrer ce soir
idea_parts: polite request → Je voudrais réserver une table
reason → parce que nous allons célébrer ce soir
exercises.target_answer: Je voudrais réserver une table parce que nous allons célébrer ce soir
exercises.meaning: I would like to reserve a table because we are going to celebrate tonight
exercises.explanation: Combines conditional je voudrais + -ation verb réserver + parce que + near future nous allons célébrer.

diagnosis.slip: used veux or forgot que after parce
diagnosis.cue: Chain Je voudrais réserver une table + parce que nous allons célébrer ce soir.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Tu as raison, c'était une excellente décision
exercises.target_answer: Tu as raison, c'était une excellente décision
exercises.meaning: You are right, it was an excellent decision
cues: You have reason: Tu as raison
it was an excellent decision: c'était une excellente décision
exercises.explanation: Synthesizes avoir raison, imparfait c'était, feminine agreement, and the -ion bridge.
exercises.affirmation: You completed the spine dictation across all five phases!

summary.outcome: Read, hear, and assemble multi-clause French sentences combining all 9 conversion bridges, tenses, and pronouns.

use_example.german: Je comprends maintenant le français que j'avais déjà dans la tête.
use_example.english: I now understand the French that I already had inside my head.

summary.takeaway: You didn't memorize a foreign language from scratch — you unlocked the French half of your own English.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([3001] A Day in Paris: Reading): see how Capstone: Le Pont Reading leads directly into A Day in Paris: Reading.

twist.prompt: Final spine twist — 'I understand the French that you speak':
twist.target_answer: Je comprends le français que tu parles
twist.explanation: Je comprends + le français + object relative que + tu parles — congratulations on crossing Le Pont!

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 29 (The French Mind) now pays off directly inside Capstone: Le Pont Reading: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

ville.etymology_derivation: Latin vīlla 'country estate' grew into the whole city in French (leaving 'city' as la cité for the historic core).

université.etymology_derivation: -ity → -ité, and every -ité is feminine. The accent on the é marks the final syllable English swallows.

liberté.etymology_derivation: liberté/liberty — the Norman doublet in -ité form: same Latin liber, two carriers.

différence.etymology_derivation: Latin differentia. The -ance/-ence endings convert whole and are always feminine.

docteur.etymology_derivation: Latin doctor 'teacher'. -or/-er nouns convert to -eur and are usually masculine.

hôtel.shift_rule: Norman doublet: S and H dropped
hôtel.etymology_derivation: Latin hospitalis → hostel AND hôtel — the same word entered English twice: once with its S (hostel, hospital), once without (hôtel).

comprendre.etymology_derivation: To understand is literally 'to grasp together'.

voudrais.context_phrase: Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
voudrais.context_translation: I would like a croissant, please.
voudrais.etymology_derivation: Future stem voudr- + imparfait ending -ais = the polite conditional!

faut.english_meaning: is necessary (il faut: one must / it is needed)
faut.context_translation: We/you have to leave now (lit. It is necessary to leave).
faut.etymology_derivation: From Latin fallere 'to be lacking' — what is lacking is what is needed! Only ever used with il.

depuis.context_translation: I have lived here for three years (lit. I live here since three years).
depuis.etymology_derivation: Because the action is still true right now, French uses the PRESENT tense with depuis!

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
